S075-01.notes: Relative pronoun is the subject of 'traveled', so 'who'. A 'whom' is object case; C 'she' creates a run-on with no link to 'woman'; D 'which' is not used for a person.

S075-02.notes: Subject 'Bayard Rustin' (with an appositive between commas) needs a finite main verb. A and C are nonfinite, so the sentence becomes a fragment; B turns the predicate into a relative clause and leaves no main verb.

S075-03.notes: A colon after a complete independent clause introduces the quoted phrase. B: a semicolon needs an independent clause after it, but a bare quotation follows. C: comma splice. D: 'that' leaves no verb, so it is ungrammatical.

S075-04.notes: 'Four years earlier' than the 1972 past event needs the past perfect 'had become'. A (present perfect), B (present) and D (future) clash with the past time frame.

S075-05.notes: 'However' interrupts 'The next year ... his medals were taken away', so it needs commas on both sides. A leaves out the second comma. C has no punctuation. D puts a semicolon after the fragment 'The next year'.

flags.note: In B the subject phrase 'the first Latin American player inducted...' refers to Clemente himself, so B is not a clear dangling modifier. It is still clearly worse than D (an indirect, awkward subject with the name delayed to the end), but it is a softer distractor than usual. Consider rewording B, e.g. 'Clemente's induction made him...'.

S075-06.notes: The opening modifier 'Honored the following year in a special election' has to attach to Clemente. A makes the Hall of Fame the one honored; C makes the special election the one honored. D puts 'Clemente' right after the modifier.

S075-07.notes: The plural subject 'findings' takes 'were', in the past (they were overlooked until 1900). A is singular. B is singular and has the wrong tense for a span that ended in 1900. D, the participle 'being', leaves no main verb.

S075-08.notes: The head noun is 'the number', which is singular, so 'is'. 'Copies' (and the plural 'survive') is the trap. B and D are plural. C is plural and its progressive tense is illogical.

S075-09.notes: 'Speed and exactness' points to 'precision'. Hesitancy, informality and fragility contradict the praise and the exact execution.

S075-10.notes: Water forms beads and rolls off, so the leaves are water-repellent. A and C are the opposite of this. B has nothing to do with the description.

S075-11.notes: The text introduces the transistor and explains why it mattered (smaller, lower power, made radios and computers practical). A contradicts the text. B: the careers are not compared. D: no design or manufacturing details are given.

S075-12.notes: The text gives the earlier belief (only some mammals), then the magpie mark test, then the result that challenges the belief. B: no flaw is mentioned. C: no natural-habitat comparison. D: no claim about relative intelligence.

S075-13.notes: Gallup offers another explanation, a parasite-seeking response. A: he does not agree that the fish recognized themselves. B: he grants that the fish see the mark in the mirror. C overstates his position ('proving', 'no fish ever').

S075-14.notes: Older females lead most often when food is scarce, which suggests they lead using knowledge of where food is. A: speed is not mentioned, and 'only' is too strong. C reverses cause and effect. D overgeneralizes with 'never'.

S075-15.notes: Computed: inside 29-31 (2 degree range) vs outside 20-35 (15 degree range); only C compares variability. A: outside data only. B: a single time point and the difference, not stability. D: inside data only, and it highlights a change.

S075-16.notes: Fewer crystalline regions linked to lower strength ties those regions directly to strength. B covers silk types. C is about stretch, not where the strength comes from. D is a general protein fact with no link to the crystalline regions.

S075-17.notes: The kingfisher observation led to a nose redesign that solved the tunnel-boom problem. A: the text does not claim this. B: 'always' is contradicted, since the trains caused booms. C: the service did not stop.

S075-18.notes: The events are in chronological order (1985, then 1987 and 1991), so 'Subsequently'. A and C imply contrast or replacement that the text does not support. D: an election is not an example of her succession.

S075-19.notes: Because nests treat one another as nestmates and do not fight, they can form a connected supercolony, which is a consequence. A and B wrongly signal contrast. D: the supercolony is a result of the behavior, not a parallel example of it.

S075-20.notes: Only A names barrier-breaking in both tennis (first Black Grand Slam champion) and golf (first Black woman on the LPGA tour). B and C are tennis only. D is golf only and leaves out 'first'.

S075-21.notes: A dash introduces the closing appositive that defines infrasound. A: what follows the semicolon is not an independent clause. C: comma splice, and 'it is ... rumbles' also has agreement trouble. D: the relative clause 'which low-pitched rumbles...' has no verb.

S075-22.notes: She saw that machines were the future, so she learned FORTRAN, an action that follows from that realization. A implies contrast, but her learning follows from it. B: there is no parallel situation. D: this is not an example.

S075-23.notes: The petition responds to the barrier (a whites-only school). A, B and C (similarity, example, restatement) do not fit.

S075-24.notes: Only B links West's Earth model to GPS and to everyday phone use. A: Hall of Fame only. C: employment history only. D: GPS only, with no mention of West.
